column5: What is the difference between a Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisor?
column6: Type 1 (bare-metal) runs directly on hardware with no host OS — examples: ESXi, KVM, Xen, Hyper-V. Type 2 (hosted) runs on top of a host OS — examples: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation. Type 1 has lower overhead and is used in datacenters and cloud. Type 2 is used for development and testing.\n\nRemember: "Hypervisor = VM manager." Type 1 (bare metal): ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM. Type 2 (hosted): VirtualBox, VMware Workstation.

column5: What are the three components of the Linux virtualization stack?
column6:
KVM (kernel module providing hardware-accelerated CPU and memory virtualization via /dev/kvm), QEMU (userspace hardware emulation for disks, NICs, USB, display), and libvirt (unified API and daemon for managing VMs — virsh, virt-manager, and Terraform all talk to libvirt).

Remember: "VM vs Container: VMs virtualize hardware (heavy, isolated), Containers share the kernel (light, fast)."

Gotcha: Containers are NOT VMs — a kernel exploit escapes all containers.

column5: Why should you always use VirtIO devices in production VMs?
column6: VirtIO is a paravirtualized framework where the guest explicitly cooperates with the hypervisor. Compared to fully emulated devices (e.g., e1000 NIC or IDE disk), VirtIO provides 2-10x better network performance and 2-5x better block storage performance because it avoids the overhead of emulating legacy hardware.

column5: What are the essential virsh commands for VM lifecycle management?
column6: virsh list --all (list VMs), virsh start/shutdown/destroy/reboot <vm> (power control), virsh suspend/resume (pause in memory), virsh console <vm> (serial console, Ctrl+] to exit), virsh dominfo/domblklist/domiflist <vm> (metadata, disks, NICs). shutdown sends ACPI signal (graceful), destroy is like pulling the power plug.

column5: Compare raw and qcow2 VM disk formats.
column6: raw: no thin provisioning, no snapshots, best I/O performance — use for high-performance workloads. qcow2: supports thin provisioning (disk grows on demand), supports snapshots, good performance — use for general purpose. qcow2 is the default choice; raw is for when maximum I/O performance is critical.

column5: How do VM snapshots work and why are they not a substitute for backups?
column6: Snapshots create a chain of differential disk images capturing a point-in-time state (virsh snapshot-create-as, snapshot-revert, snapshot-delete). They are not backups because the chain degrades performance as it grows, they reside on the same storage as the VM, and they are meant for short-term rollback points (hours, not weeks).

column5: What are the prerequisites and steps for live migration of a VM?
column6: Prerequisites: shared storage (NFS, Ceph, GlusterFS) or use --copy-storage-all, same CPU architecture on both hosts, network connectivity, libvirtd on both hosts. Steps: memory pages iteratively copied to destination, VM briefly paused when dirty page rate converges, remaining state (CPU registers, device state) transferred, VM resumes on destination. Typical downtime: 10-200ms.

column5: Why does NUMA-aware VM placement matter and how do you configure it?
column6: Modern multi-socket servers have Non-Uniform Memory Access — CPUs have fast local memory and slow remote memory (40-100ns extra latency per access). Pin a VM's vCPUs and memory to the same NUMA node using virsh vcpupin <vm> <vcpu> <cpu> and virsh numatune <vm> --mode strict --nodeset 0. Cross-node access kills latency-sensitive workloads.

column5: How does memory ballooning work in virtualization?
column6: The virtio-balloon driver lets the hypervisor reclaim memory from guests dynamically. virsh setmem <vm> 2G --live inflates the balloon (guest sees less RAM, hypervisor reclaims the rest). virsh setmem <vm> 6G --live deflates it (gives memory back). The guest kernel handles the reduced memory by swapping or reclaiming cache. Maximum memory is set with virsh setmaxmem.

column5: How does VMware ESXi differ from KVM in enterprise environments?
column6: ESXi is a proprietary Type 1 hypervisor (free tier available, features require vSphere license). It uses vCenter for multi-host management (equivalent to oVirt for KVM), VMFS or vSAN for storage (vs qcow2/raw), and vMotion for live migration. CLI access via esxcli and vim-cmd. \nKey difference: ESXi is a managed product with enterprise support; KVM is open-source with community tooling.
